		<title>Why Package Digital Twins Are So Hard To Build</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/why-package-digital-twins-are-so-hard-to-build/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/why-package-digital-twins-are-so-hard-to-build/#respond</comments>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Models need to be synchronized with what manufacturing actually builds.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-package-digital-twins-are-so-hard-to-build/">Why Package Digital Twins Are So Hard To Build</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Package twins must track what manufacturing actually builds, not just design intent.</li>
<li>Missing process and supplier data can undermine otherwise precise simulations.</li>
<li>Coupled physics and ongoing calibration keep models tied to physical reality.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>A chiplet can be fully characterized, tested, and considered known good, but none of that guarantees it will stay that way after it’s placed into a different package. While the chiplet itself may be unchanged, nearly everything around it can move.</p>
<p>A different substrate can alter the mechanical and electrical environment, a different thermal interface can change how heat leaves the device, and a new power envelope can increase how much heat needs to leave in the first place. A thermal path that worked in the first product can cause throttling in the second because the surrounding package and cooling assumptions have changed.</p>
<p>By the time the chiplet is assembled into another package, engineers may be dealing with a different system altogether, which is why package models can’t stop at the die boundary, and why the added complexity makes package digital twins so difficult to achieve. That is the basic problem facing digital twins for advanced packaging. They have to predict how known components will behave after integration and eventually inside a larger system.</p>
<p>“A chiplet may be characterized and validated in one package or product SKU, then reused in a different package stack, substrate, cooling approach, or power envelope,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “The chiplet has not changed, but its electrical, thermal, and mechanical environment has.”</p>
<p><strong>Fab vs. packaging: A different kind of twin</strong><br />
Digital twins are starting to be used in semiconductor manufacturing, but the comparison with front-end fabs needs some clarification. A fab process twin can be enormously complicated, incorporating equipment behavior, process history, and statistical learning. The difference is that much of that complexity remains inside a relatively well-defined manufacturing environment.</p>
<p>“A fab process twin is extremely complex, so I would not frame this as fab being easy and package being hard,” Larsen said. “The difference is the nature of the problem. A fab twin is usually deep within one manufacturing environment, one process technology, and one managed flow of equipment, materials, process data, and statistical learning. A package digital twin has to solve a broader integration problem — how a multi-die system is realized across silicon, substrate, assembly, manufacturing variation, test, and reliability learning.”</p>
<p>That broader integration problem changes what the twin has to represent. In heterogeneous integration, the package is increasingly part of the system architecture, so electrical, thermal and mechanical behavior cannot be optimized independently. Engineers already have effective tools for each of those domains, but they don’t become a package twin simply by running next to one another.</p>
<p>The harder problem is keeping them synchronized around the same physical package as it moves from design to manufacturing. Manufacturing results also need to feed back into those models as the package is revised.</p>
<p>“The package, silicon, substrate, materials, thermal solution, and manufacturing assumptions have to be explored together,” Larsen said. “If they are optimized separately, the digital twin becomes a late-stage validation artifact. That is not where the value is.”</p>
<p>The boundary also becomes less obvious once the package moves onto a board and into its eventual system. Conditions outside the package can change its behavior, which means some of that context has to travel with the model.</p>
<p>“An end-to-end package digital twin requires visibility across the entire lifecycle, from wafer fabrication through assembly, test, and ultimately system operation,” said Joon Ahn, vice president of global factory IT and automation at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/amkor-technology/">Amkor</a>. “Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.”</p>
<p>Preserving that context would be difficult even if all of the necessary information were sitting in one place. Often, it’s not.</p>
<p><strong>The data hole</strong><br />
From the OSAT perspective, much of the information needed to describe an advanced package comes from elsewhere. Some of it comes from the foundry, some from substrate and material suppliers, and some is generated only after assembly or test. Even equipment inside the same manufacturing flow may provide different types of data depending on its age and supplier.</p>
<p>“For OSATs, an end-to-end digital twin is not a single model, but a connected ecosystem of process, equipment, production, supply chain, and traceability data,” said Ahn. “Packaging performance is influenced by interactions among multiple process steps. Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.”</p>
<p>What an OSAT receives can be quite different from what a predictive model ideally contains. Incoming die data may include critical dimensions and wafer-sort results, but not detailed power-density or local stress maps. A substrate may arrive within nominal specifications without showing actual warpage across the production lot, while material data sheets may not capture material-specific behavior in the end device.</p>
<p>“The downstream analysis can then look precise while missing the manufacturing reality,” Larsen said. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.”</p>
<p>That context can be lost even when plenty of data survives the handoff. The problem is that different parts of the supply chain may describe the same physical system in different ways.</p>
<p>“The hardest handoffs aren’t necessarily where we have the least data. They’re usually where the data has to move between very different engineering domains,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&amp;D at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/ase/">ASE</a>. “A foundry may describe die behavior one way, a substrate supplier another, and a materials company may provide properties measured under a very specific set of conditions. Then the OSAT has to bring all of that together and understand how it will behave during assembly.”</p>
<p>That context becomes even harder to preserve when the information crosses company boundaries. The material supplier knows things about the chemistry that the equipment company doesn’t. The equipment company knows details of the process integration that may not be available to the OSAT or fab. Much of that knowledge also represents intellectual property.</p>
<p>“We all have our own data and everybody wants to protect intellectual property,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of marketing and business development at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mitsubishi-chemical-group/">Mitsubishi Chemical Group</a>. “I’ve been in this industry all my life, and when we started we had a different way of collaborating. We were a lot more open as an industry, as an ecosystem.”</p>
<p>For a package digital twin, this makes the data problem partly technical and partly organizational. A common file format can help move information between tools, but it can’t provide process data that was never shared, a material property that was never characterized, or an excursion that occurred farther upstream and was not attached to the incoming die. The model can be incomplete before the first coupled simulation is run.</p>
<p><strong>Manufacturing gets a vote</strong><br />
Even complete nominal data only describes the package engineers intended to fabricate. Manufacturing still gets a vote, and it doesn’t always vote for the nominal geometry. The difference is particularly visible in photonics, where relatively small shifts in geometry can materially alter device behavior. Critical dimensions, film thickness, or sidewall profile can move enough during processing to change optical loss or wavelength response without anything being obviously “broken.”</p>
<p>“The biggest disconnect is that photonic devices are typically designed and optimized using idealized geometries, while manufactured devices are governed by process-induced variability,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/">Silvaco’s</a> TCAD business unit. “A photonic integrated circuit may demonstrate excellent performance in simulation or in a carefully controlled research run, but high-volume manufacturing introduces variations in dimensions, profiles, and materials that directly affect optical behavior. As a result, a design optimized for the ‘as-drawn’ geometry often does not represent the ‘as-manufactured’ device.'&#8221;</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281380" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Greg.jpg?resize=1430%2C605&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1430" height="605" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Greg.jpg?w=1430&amp;ssl=1 1430w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Greg.jpg?resize=300%2C127&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Greg.jpg?resize=1024%2C433&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Greg.jpg?resize=768%2C325&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Greg.jpg?resize=600%2C254&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: GPU-powered 3D FDTD (finite-difference time domain) simulation shows variations in the resulting electric field due to manufacturing variations. Source: Silvaco</strong></p>
<p>The same problem extends beyond photonics. The model may describe the nominal structure correctly while missing a manufacturing effect that appeared secondary until the hardware is built.</p>
<p>“Subtle nuances don’t show up in the model,” said Brad Booth, CEO of NLM Photonics. “We’ve kind of done this with ASIC design tools. We can simulate stuff first, and what you get out of the back end is usually very close to what you represented in a software model. When you start bringing in things that haven’t had that level of lifetime or qualification, or if you’re pushing the bleeding edge, it’s a little harder because now you’re introducing subtleties, and those subtleties can have massive impacts.”</p>
<p>Fine process details such as humidity levels, changes in cleaning chemistry concentration, or a slight under-etch become model inputs if they change performance. New materials add another complication because engineers need to know not only their nominal properties, but how those properties change with dimension, environment (especially temperature), and time.</p>
<p>“A datasheet gives you a snapshot — CTE, modulus, adhesion, viscosity, measured under one set of conditions at one point in time,” said Hanlin Chen, research scientist and team lead at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/brewer-science/">Brewer Science</a>. “Mechanical and thermal properties shift with the degree of curing. Crosslink density may continue to evolve after processing, and adhesion strength depends heavily on the specific bonding interface. CTE also varies, particularly in the temperature region near the polymer’s Tg [glass transition temperature]. Treating any of these as a single static number causes a lot of simulation-to-silicon gaps.”</p>
<p>That creates a moving target even when the material name and formulation have not changed. A value that was accurate when the model was built may become less representative after cure, thermal exposure, or assembly. So the problem is not simply about collecting more material properties. Engineers also must know when those properties apply.</p>
<p>“When you introduce any new material into that, it just explodes the number of knobs and dials, because you’ve got to know how that material performs in all these different environments and what its variance is over its lifetime,” Booth said. “You can model to a certain level and say, ‘This is the ballpark I should be in.’ But then you actually have to build the parts because you have to have some way to correlate back to that model.”</p>
<p>Building the parts settles one question and immediately creates another. Once new materials are assembled, their variations stop behaving independently. At that point, building the twin is no longer mainly a matter of adding better inputs. It also involves changes caused by the thermal and mechanical environment.</p>
<p><strong>When one problem becomes another</strong><br />
That interaction is where package digital twins begin to depart most sharply from a collection of conventional simulations. Engineers may model thermal, mechanical, and electrical behavior separately for expediency, but the physical package doesn’t respect those boundaries.</p>
<p>Once those effects begin feeding back into one another, separate models become harder to keep separate. Power is a straightforward example. Current creates heat, heat changes resistance, and those electrical changes alter the power being dissipated. The new power distribution changes the thermal picture again, so engineers may have to iterate between electrical and thermal models until the results converge.</p>
<p>The same problem can happen in process variation, where one change can alter the effect of another rather than simply adding to it.</p>
<p>“A key observation is that these variables rarely act independently,” said Silvaco’s Guichard. “Yield is often limited by the combined and nonlinear interaction of multiple process variations.”</p>
<p>This is also where standardization gets difficult. Models for heat transfer or electrical behavior may be well understood on their own, but the assumptions used at the interfaces are less portable.</p>
<p>“The least-standardized models are often at the interfaces, not in the isolated physics domains,” Synopsys’ Larsen said. “The difficult areas are where materials, structures, processes, suppliers, and system-level decisions meet.”</p>
<p>A substrate supplier and an assembly house may both have technically valid models, for example, while describing different parts of the same physical behavior under different assumptions. The problem is not necessarily that either model is wrong but they may not mesh cleanly enough to produce a common representation of the package.</p>
<p><strong>Calibration never ends</strong><br />
Eventually, the physical package gets a chance to argue with the model. When it does, the measurements become part of the twin itself rather than a final check. Intel’s hybrid-bonding work offers a useful example. Experimental distortion data is fed back into the finite-element model, which engineers can then refine before using it to explore changes that would be impractical to test experimentally.</p>
<p>The goal is to narrow the range of conditions engineers need to explore to reduce distortion and eventually understand how sensitive that behavior is to changes in process and materials, because one measurement rarely tells the whole story. Warpage is an obvious calibration target for advanced packaging, but meeting a warpage target doesn’t show that everything else in the package is behaving as expected.</p>
<p>The harder question is deciding when another measurement is actually needed. Following every variable through every process step would quickly become impractical, but some manufacturing steps alter the package&#8217;s physical state enough that the model needs another reality check.</p>
<p>“I don’t think the answer is to measure everything at every step,” said ASE’s Hung. “It’s really about measuring at the points where the package changes state.” Those transitions can include bonding, molding, curing, thinning, and thermal transitions.</p>
<p>For this reason, modeling has to consider all package interfaces and test results. “For a package model, warpage is the obvious measurement, but it is not enough,” said Amkor’s Ahn. “The calibration set has to include bump and interconnect metrology, die placement, substrate characterization, underfill/mold/TIM measurements, thermal characterization measurements, and electrical testing.”</p>
<p>Model development and physical development therefore cannot be separated when the technology itself is new.</p>
<p>“You’ve got to build that twin at the same time you’re building the devices, so you have some correlation,” NLM’s Booth said. “We’re having to literally do both of those in lockstep, because as much as I can go and create this thing and say, ‘Here’s this great circuit,’ until I’ve actually built one and shown that I can build it and it equates to what was in the digital twin, I can’t really say that my digital twin is an accurate representation of the end product.”</p>
<p>Nor does a successful calibration remain valid indefinitely. A change in the package, materials, or process can push the next application beyond the conditions used to validate the original model.</p>
<p>“There’s no fixed interval; it’s driven by how far the new application sits from the conditions of the original model,” said Brewer Science&#8217;s Chen. “A new package architecture, a different substrate, a shift in thermal budget, or a change in process flow can all move a material outside its validated envelope. Our approach is to recalibrate whenever the customer’s application introduces a meaningful change in those variables, rather than on a calendar schedule.”</p>
<p>Calibration also has its limits. It is only useful as long as the conditions that made the model valid remain attached to it. That becomes particularly important with reduced-order and AI surrogate models, where speed depends on using a simplified representation without losing track of the conditions under which it remains trustworthy.</p>
<p>“Without that context, a fast model can become a fast way to make the wrong decision,” Larsen said.</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion: Keeping the twin attached to reality</strong><br />
The difficulty in building a package digital twin goes beyond creating accurate electrical, thermal, or mechanical models. The challenge is keeping those models attached to the same physical package as manufacturing changes it and new information becomes available. Measurements from fabrication, assembly, and test have to feed back into the representation, along with enough context to show what those measurements actually describe.</p>
<p>That is particularly difficult in advanced packaging because there may never be a point when everything is completely known. Components come from different suppliers, materials change during processing, and assembly introduces new stresses and interactions. The twin has to evolve along with the package or risk becoming a precise model of something that no longer exists.</p>
<p>“A useful package twin is not just a simulation sitting next to the hardware,” Larsen said. “The built package should improve the model, and the model should let teams ask what will change before they commit to the next design, package stack, or product SKU.”</p>
<p>That may be the real measure of success. The twin does not have to predict the physical package perfectly once. It has to remain useful as the physical package changes.</p>

		<title>Negative Expansion Materials Resist Warpage</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/negative-expansion-materials-resist-warpage/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/negative-expansion-materials-resist-warpage/#respond</comments>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Molding compounds and underfill can improve thermal stability.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/negative-expansion-materials-resist-warpage/">Negative Expansion Materials Resist Warpage</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Warpage is becoming a bigger constraint as package, interposer, and panel sizes grow.</li>
<li>Negative thermal expansion (NTE) materials, newly on the market, can help counter warpage.</li>
<li>Commercial NTE materials are starting to be used in semiconductor packaging, but broader adoption will depend on temperature range, compatibility of different materials, and uniform mixing and purity.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Thermally induced warpage, caused by differences in the rate at which materials expand when heated, is becoming increasingly problematic in large chips and packages. The solution may be to integrate a new class of materials that actually shrink when heated.</p>
<p>Rather than relying solely on the few substances that can shrink, companies are focusing on mixtures of materials with a lattice structure that can resist the urge to expand. Using such materials for underfill and as the packaging molding compound can add rigidity for larger packages while keeping warpage in check.</p>
<p><strong>Warpage as the enemy</strong><br />
Warpage, especially in large packages and panels, occurs because of mismatches between how, for example, a substrate, a die, and surrounding molding compound behave when heated. It’s one of the biggest issues holding back the constant enlargement of package substrates, interposers, and panels. The larger the bonded area, the greater the likelihood that edge connections may be poor or fail altogether. Even before bonding, too much warpage can defeat standard manufacturing equipment features such as vacuum chucks.</p>
<p>“The vacuum chucks will pull the warpage down, but if the warpage is too high, then you won&#8217;t get a good vacuum,” said Knowlton Olmstead, senior manager of wafer services at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/amkor-technology/">Amkor</a>.</p>
<p>Anywhere two materials meet with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE), warping is likely to some degree. For example, given two layers of material, if the bottom layer has a higher CTE, then it will try to expand to its natural extent. But the material above it will restrict it, assuming they’re well adhered. That will cause the edges of the bottom material to want to curl up.</p>
<p>It’s theoretically impossible to stop all warpage if there is a CTE difference. The question becomes how much is too much. If it’s too much, what can you do about it?</p>
<p>“We do a certain level of modeling to model the warpage beforehand, and then there&#8217;s certain levers you can pull to control the warpage,” said Olmstead.</p>
<p>If silicon is one of the layers (as it often is), thinning the silicon can reduce the amount of warping. “You reduce the impact of the low CTE silicon if there&#8217;s thinner silicon,” said Mike Kelly, vice president, chiplets/FCBGA integration at Amkor. “In the extreme, you can make it super thin, and then it can follow the shape of whatever I&#8217;m attached to. But that ends up being a problem, because nobody wants really thin silicon for managing high power.”</p>
<p>Warpage also impacts how new materials may be received, such as glass. “The larger the panel you&#8217;re trying to make, the more warpage you will see,” said Lang Lin, principal product manager at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “Today we talk about micrometers of warpage, but with glass, it could be even larger — millimeters, maybe.”</p>
<p>One approach being explored is to identify or design materials that contract when heated, giving them a negative CTE.</p>
<p>“Negative CTE materials could be utilized in a variety of ways to offset expansion,” said Luke Prenger, research scientist IV team lead at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/brewer-science/">Brewer Science</a>. “It might depend on why the expansion needs to be offset to begin with. For things like stress management and warpage reduction, negative CTE materials can be utilized to help better match the CTEs of different materials. An example case of this would be to add filler to a polymer material, which typically has a very high CTE compared to inorganics, to reduce the overall CTE of the polymer matrix so it is closer to that of the metal layers and other components in the device. Reducing or modulating the CTE of organic layers to be closer to the inorganic layers helps in reducing warpage and overall stress build-up in a device.”</p>
<p><strong>Going against the grain</strong><br />
One of the material interfaces that results in warping is the epoxy molding compound (EMC) used for fillers and underfill. It fills all the major gaps inside the package, so when the temperature changes, it can affect everything it touches. Altering the composition of that compound can mitigate the warping. The key is changing the CTE, with a negative CTE ideal for counteracting an adjacent positive one. Alternatively, mixing a positive CTE material with a negative one can alter the overall CTE of the combination.</p>
<p>A variety of materials can exhibit true negative thermal expansion (NTE) behavior, although it often occurs within specific temperature ranges. It may also be associated with a phase change. For example, water behaves normally above 3.98 °C, below which it moves toward freezing. Ice is famously less dense than water due to its molecular structure, and so as more of the water takes on that configuration between 3.98°C and 0°C, it expands up until the final phase transition to ice.</p>
<p>Unlike materials exhibiting true NTE behavior, other substances may consist of normal materials encased in a lattice that restricts expansion. The structure of that lattice is important in determining how anything encased in it behaves.</p>
<p>“The key is the structure of the filler itself,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of global marketing and business development for the semiconductor business at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mitsubishi-chemical-group/">Mitsubishi Chemical Group</a>.</p>
<p>Solids may have a wide range of molecular arrangements. Whereas polymers can be amorphous, inorganic materials typically have some sort of lattice structure. Materials scientists categorize the different structures and study their rheological properties (which refers to the study of how they flow).</p>
<p>They’ll describe lattice structures, such as house-of-cards, rigid-rod, or tetrahedral. Each of these structures behave differently and can establish rigidity in one or more dimensions. What’s within the lattice (also called a matrix or a network) can also affect the flow, and the combined NTE materials reflect such a structure — a functional material within a restraining matrix.</p>
<p>“It’s more of a network thing than a material thing,” explained Bhatt. “Not everything will form the same network. A carbon powder forms a flocculated network. If you look at a carbon fiber network, that is a reinforcing rigid-rod network. So if you are going to put a carbon fiber into a matrix, it’s like logs in a river. If I use the logs in water, it is going to have little impact on the ability of water to flow. It will restrict it some, but the water is still going to find room between them. If I put a whole bunch of clay in the water, it will muddy it up, and it will literally restrict the water movement because now you have changed the viscosity.”</p>
<p><strong>Caught in a cage</strong><br />
Such a structure, a matrix encasing another material, can restrict the tendency for the enclosed substance to expand. It can even contract a little when heated by reorienting the molecules in the structure. Rheologically, expansion and contraction are studied as flows, so in the restricted case, the flow is redirected in a way that avoids the warpage that might otherwise occur.</p>
<p>“A lot of people will talk about shrinkage and expansion, but to me, those are low shear-rate flows rheologically,” said Bhatt. “If you&#8217;re looking at something in a matrix, when you heat it up, the reason it shrinks or expands is because it has to flow. The molecules want to relax. That flow finds the easiest path. Now you integrate something to cage it. Then you change the dynamics of that flow.”</p>
<p>“In these [filler] materials you have a house-of-cards, so it’s a lattice that does not allow movement, and the network arranges itself so the resultant matrix turns out to have a negative CTE,” Bhatt said. “Self-assembly is where chemistry comes into the picture — you have to make sure that these things are functionalized appropriately so they arrange themselves in a certain way.”</p>
<p>Having one material trying to expand but being restrained by another structure raises the question of whether the matrix could ever burst under pressure from the expanding material. The answer is yes. This is called melting, at which point the entire configuration falls apart.</p>
<p>“If you have a matrix and you melt it and it starts flowing, that&#8217;s the bursting analogy,” he said.  “But by that time, the material has the matrix thermal capability.”</p>
<p>Even though this matrix changes the flow characteristics of the material it encases, it doesn’t change the characteristic temperatures of that material. “The reinforcement does very little for the thermal transitional behavior of the matrix material,” noted Bhatt. “It will never change the glass transition or the melt transition temperature.”</p>
<p>This also isn’t about establishing a zero-CTE material. The idea is to tune the compound&#8217;s CTE to minimize differences between one material and another.</p>
<p>“Our negative-CTE filler contracts as temperature rises, offsetting the natural expansion of the resin,” said Bhatt. “By lowering and tuning the effective CTE of the molding compound, it reduces thermal-expansion mismatch among the die, substrate, and encapsulant, helping minimize stress and package warpage.”</p>
<p><strong>NTE materials debut</strong><br />
NTE materials are unusual, which is a downside. “The number of negative CTE materials is very limited,” confirmed Prenger. “β-eucryptite is actively used as ceramics for chunks and parts in certain tooling, and zirconium tungstate is being utilized as an additive for various types of mold compounds and underfills.”</p>
<p>While eucryptite (meaning “well concealed&#8221;) is found in nature (if you look hard enough, apparently), zirconium tungstate is not. With NTE in all three dimensions, it’s one of the human-made NTE substances. Such materials are very challenging to design.</p>
<p>“On top of negative CTE materials already having a limited selection, designing new materials is very complicated and exists only in the realm of inorganic materials,” explained Prenger. “For organic materials, for almost every polymer material that is noted to have negative CTE, it is negative only in one dimension, not in three dimensions. This leads to organic materials being exclusively limited to adding inorganic fillers.”</p>
<p>Although NTE materials have been a research topic for a while, they’ve recently become available from Mitsubishi Chemical Group. It’s an inorganic material that can be mixed with organic epoxy resins to customize the epoxy&#8217;s CTE. It’s also available pre-mixed with resin.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281400" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Bryon.jpg?resize=953%2C638&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="953" height="638" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Bryon.jpg?w=953&amp;ssl=1 953w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Bryon.jpg?resize=300%2C201&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Bryon.jpg?resize=768%2C514&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MPM-Bryon.jpg?resize=600%2C402&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 953px) 100vw, 953px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Mitsubishi Chemical’s NTE material can be mixed into epoxy resins for electronics packaging. Source: Mitsubishi Chemical Group</strong></p>
<p>If this proves out and other materials companies follow suit, this could become a standard formulation for semiconductor packaging. But for commercial success, these materials must perform over a wide temperature range to cover not only processing but also higher-temperature manufacturing operations. They must be easily and uniformly mixed into resins. They must also not introduce unexpected effects from alpha-particle emissions caused by impurities.</p>
<p>If all works as planned, this may be yet another step toward enabling larger packages and panels.</p>
<p><strong>— Gregory Haley contributed to this article.</strong></p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Intel may be the marquee name, but materials suppliers, packaging hubs, and quantum startups will determine whether the region becomes a true semiconductor ecosystem.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-silicon-heartland-wants-to-be-americas-next-chip-powerhouse/">The Silicon Heartland Wants To Be America’s Next Chip Powerhouse</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Major facility investments are driving momentum for the Midwestern semiconductor industry.</li>
<li>Workforce development remains a major structural challenge.</li>
<li>Quantum investment in Chicago represents a major opportunity for the regional semiconductor ecosystem.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>The U.S. semiconductor industry has long been concentrated in established technology and manufacturing hubs, but new investments and startup activity are helping expand the industry&#8217;s footprint across the Midwest.</p>
<p>The prospect of a thriving Midwestern semiconductor industry has long hinged on whether semiconductor companies can leverage the region’s strong base of research institutions and available workforce, logistics, and industrial infrastructure to build a regional ecosystem. Over the last several years, that trend has gained momentum, with <a href="https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/corporate-responsibility/intel-in-ohio.html">Intel</a> and <a href="https://www.skhynix.com/westlafayette.IN/">SK hynix</a> bringing landmark facility investments to the Midwest, major bets on the future of quantum computing being made on the shores of Lake Michigan, and significant government investment being funneled toward semiconductor growth and startup support.</p>
<p><strong>Defining the Midwestern ecosystem</strong><br />
The Midwest has undergone something of a “transformation” in recent years, with signs of a real semiconductor ecosystem beginning to materialize. “There&#8217;s always been this culture of innovation, but because a lot of the semiconductor and microelectronics work had existed on the coasts, or had been elsewhere, while the Midwest was really the heart for manufacturing, there&#8217;s been this transformation to a technology-based silicon heartland ecosystem,” said Matt Casto, CEO of Midwest Microelectronics Consortium (MMEC). “New foundry capabilities are being built just north of Columbus, Ohio. Supply chain manufacturers range from water treatment capabilities to semiconductor tools. We&#8217;ve got companies in the Midwest and in the state of Ohio now that are doing material growth development. So the building blocks for semiconductor work can connect within that Midwest ecosystem through additional supply chain capabilities. Now is a generational opportunity around advanced technology, and that requires a lot more emphasis on workforce development.”</p>
<p>The vision for this developing semiconductor ecosystem rests on a diverse technology production network that can integrate into the region’s existing manufacturing and research base. “One defining characteristic of the Midwest is its emphasis on connecting semiconductor innovation directly to manufacturing and industrial applications,” said Christopher Salomone, account management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “While some regions are heavily concentrated in either semiconductor design or fabrication, the Midwest is building a more integrated ecosystem that includes research institutions, advanced manufacturing, automotive technology, defense applications, and emerging semiconductor production capabilities.”</p>
<p>One of the biggest markers of the industry’s Midwestern development has been Intel’s <a href="https://siliconheartland.newalbanyohio.org/">$28B+ “Silicon Heartland”</a> project in suburban Central Ohio. Expected to open in the early 2030s, the facility will create 3,000 new Intel jobs in the metro Columbus area once fully operational.</p>
<p>“Intel&#8217;s investment helped establish the Midwest as a serious contender in advanced semiconductor manufacturing and created opportunities that simply didn&#8217;t exist in this region before,” said Ted Geer, director of state government affairs for Ohio at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/intel-foundry/">Intel</a>. “The Midwest has always produced exceptional engineers, researchers, and technical talent through its universities and research institutions. Too often, however, many of those graduates built their careers elsewhere. Today, students and researchers across the region can see a pathway to participate in leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing without leaving the Midwest. Organizations like MMEC are helping build on that momentum by strengthening connections between research, talent development, and the future of domestic microelectronics.”</p>
<p>Part of the growing momentum also comes from established regional power players expanding their footprint with long-term growth in mind. “Brewer Science has been rooted in the Midwest since 1981, and our positioning isn&#8217;t incidental to the region; it&#8217;s strategic,” said Srikanth Kommu, co-CEO at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/brewer-science/">Brewer Science</a>. “We&#8217;ve demonstrated that world-class materials innovation and manufacturing can thrive outside traditional coastal hubs, which directly challenges the historical consolidation of semiconductor ecosystems. When you connect that kind of regional leadership to what we&#8217;re doing on the ground, like our acquisition of Heraeus Epurio&#8217;s semiconductor chemicals business, which brought a production facility in Dayton, Ohio, into our operations, you start to see a materials corridor forming across the Midwest that didn&#8217;t exist five years ago. Our deliberate geographic deepening through acquisitions and internal growth, from Rolla to Vichy to Springfield to now Dayton, treats our supply chain and workforce as strategic assets. This model lets us sustain margins while investing in facility upgrades, process improvements, and worker development. The manufacturers who will matter most in this region are those treating this as a 20-year investment in institutional capability, not a response to quarterly performance metrics.”</p>

<p>Still, long-standing workforce challenges remain a hurdle to the industry’s potential to reshape the regional economy.</p>
<p><strong>Filling the gaps in workforce development and funding</strong><br />
While encouraging activities are underway, the Midwest’s industry identity isn’t completely defined yet. “Every successful technology cluster develops its own identity and strengths over time,” said Intel&#8217;s Geer. “The Midwest brings a unique combination of engineering talent, manufacturing expertise, practicality, and a culture that values collaboration and getting things done. As global demand for semiconductors continues to grow, we&#8217;ll have an opportunity to see how those Midwestern strengths shape the industry&#8217;s future. Semiconductors are foundational to artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and many of the technologies that power the modern economy. I believe the Midwest has real potential to become a leading center for semiconductor innovation and manufacturing.”</p>
<p>The two biggest obstacles to the Midwestern semiconductor industry becoming a reality are existing gaps in workforce development and sustainable capital funding. “Two challenges will determine whether this regional resurgence becomes durable: workforce velocity and capital market confidence. The Midwest needs to train and develop technicians, process engineers, and materials scientists faster than any regional initiative has previously managed,” Brewer Science&#8217;s Kommu said. “The gap between supply and demand will tighten significantly. This requires sustained investment in community college partnerships, apprenticeship programs, and industry-sponsored training, a 10-to-15-year commitment with uncertain ROI. On capital, public investment is substantial, but private capital deployment will determine sustainability. If private-sector growth follows the funding cycles of government initiatives, rather than organic market demand, the region risks boom-bust dynamics that damage competitiveness. We need self-sustaining business models that generate sufficient returns to reinvest, not ongoing subsidy dependence.”</p>
<p>Then, for the industry to scale regionally, the talent pool and capital support must grow alongside demand. “Talent development will be critical to sustaining long-term growth,” said Salomone. “Another important question is how effectively the industry can translate today&#8217;s public and private investments into a durable ecosystem that remains globally competitive over the next decade. Success will depend on continued collaboration between industry, academia, and government, as well as the ability to accelerate innovation while maintaining supply chain security and economic sustainability.”</p>
<p>These structural challenges are also driving creative strategies. “I don&#8217;t think we have all the answers, but I&#8217;d point to a few things we&#8217;ve done at Brewer Science that I believe are part of the answer,” Kommu said. “We became a Certified Employee-Owned company in 2020, which means the people doing the work also have a direct stake in the company&#8217;s success. That&#8217;s a meaningful lever for retention in a tight technical labor market. We&#8217;ve also chosen, deliberately, to grow by deepening our footprint in the Midwest rather than chasing the lowest-cost location every time. The companies that answer these workforce and capital questions well will be the ones that treat their people and their supply chain as long-term investments rather than variable costs. That&#8217;s the model we&#8217;re building here, and it&#8217;s a model other Midwest manufacturers can learn from.”</p>
<p><strong>Quantum opportunities </strong><br />
The Midwest’s semiconductor industry may be well behind its coastal peers in many spheres of maturity, but there’s a concerted effort to avoid that fate when it comes to profiting from emerging quantum technologies. The Chicagoland region stands out as a hub for quantum investment, with $500 million in Illinois state <a href="https://www.psiquantum.com/news-import/illinois-iqmp">funding</a> for the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park and a planned <a href="https://gov-pritzker-newsroom.prezly.com/gov-pritzker-announces-location-and-psiquantum-as-anchor-tenant-of-new-quantum-park">$1 billion investment</a> from PsiQuantum.</p>
<p>The University of Chicago-affiliated Chicago Quantum Exchange projects that emerging quantum technology could generate up to <a href="https://chicagoquantum.org/economicimpactdata">$80B in economic impact</a> for Illinois, Wisconsin, and Indiana by 2035.</p>
<p>Quantum investment in the region is anchored by the planned <a href="https://iqmp.org/">Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park</a>, which will house companies like IBM and PsiQuantum to conduct research on quantum applications for the pharmaceutical, chemistry, energy, defense, and other industries. The project will be built on part of the former U.S. Steel site on Chicago’s south side lakefront.</p>
<p>These investments put the Midwest in a globally competitive position. “The global economic trajectory for quantum information science and engineering has increased substantially and is expected to keep growing. If the Midwest keeps its foot on the pedal and continues launching initiatives 18 to 24 months ahead of others, the region can maintain its advantage,” said Kate Waimey Timmerman, CEO of the Chicago Quantum Exchange. “We have not often done that in other sectors. Many industries are already mature enough that it would be difficult for the Midwest to become a top two ecosystem, but quantum is still open. We are consistently listed among the leading U.S. quantum ecosystems. That said, this should not be viewed as a state-by-state competition. Quantum technology is a global undertaking, and there should be more collaboration across regions.”</p>
<p>Timmerman noted that Chicago has the research base and recently has begun turning it into real opportunity. The CQE also manages the Duality Accelerator, a startup incubator program that gives companies worldwide access to hard-to-come-by quantum infrastructure.</p>
<p>“In 2020 and 2021, we launched Duality as the first quantum-focused startup accelerator in the United States,” she said. “The portfolio spans quantum computing, communications, sensing, and enabling technologies. The enabling category is especially important because the quantum supply chain includes materials, components, subsystems, and full systems. As companies mature, they may move up that stack — from individual products to subsystems and, in some cases, complete systems. To date, Duality has supported roughly 25 to 30 startups. Some are homegrown. Some came to the region for the program and then moved here permanently. qBraid is one example. Others may not relocate entirely, but they keep an employee or office here because of the ecosystem. Still others return home after the program while maintaining research and talent connections in the region.”</p>
<p>The development of quantum infrastructure offers opportunities for semiconductor companies with roots in the region. “Quantum computing represents one of the most exciting long-term opportunities in advanced computing, and the Midwest&#8217;s growing research activity in this area is encouraging,” said Synopsys’ Salomone. “While quantum systems require fundamentally different architectures than conventional computing, they still rely on sophisticated design methodologies, simulation technologies, and increasingly complex semiconductor components. As quantum technologies mature, collaboration between hardware developers, research institutions, and technology providers will be essential. Synopsys sees opportunities to support the broader ecosystem through design, modeling, verification, and system development capabilities that help accelerate innovation and reduce development complexity. We believe the research leadership emerging from Midwestern institutions can contribute meaningfully to the future of quantum and hybrid computing technologies.”</p>
<p>Timmerman points to three broad opportunities for regional companies entering the quantum space:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>For quantum technology developers</strong>: “Researchers at universities today may start companies tomorrow, and within two to five years those companies may be hiring significant numbers of people. That is the path from research to commercial opportunity in the region.”</li>
<li><strong>For manufacturers</strong>: “We think about that in two ways — helping quantum developers move from bespoke research and development to scaled manufacturing, and making this region a destination where established manufacturers can join a domestic quantum supply chain that does not yet fully exist. We already have regional manufacturers producing materials such as diamond, as well as components such as vacuum systems and nanopositioners. There is an opportunity to help those companies scale and to reach additional manufacturers that may not yet understand quantum, the emerging supply chain, or where they could fit within it.”</li>
<li><strong>For end users</strong>: “Quantum sensors are already at relatively high technology-readiness levels, and companies can buy and pilot systems today. Quantum networking and quantum computing are farther off. But this region should be among the fastest places to adopt quantum technologies because of the surrounding research and industry adjacencies. We were not necessarily at the forefront of early artificial-intelligence adoption, though that may be changing. With quantum, we have an opportunity to lead from the beginning.”</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Startup support</strong><br />
Quantum startups are not the only new ventures getting institutional support in the Midwest. EDA companies, for example, have always provided tools and expertise to educational institutions, but in the past the goal was to hire new engineering graduates and relocate them back to existing tech hubs. What&#8217;s changed is that many new jobs are being created outside of those established hubs, where the cost of living is far lower than in places like Silicon Valley.</p>
<p>“Our role is to empower startups, universities, established manufacturers, and government-supported initiatives with the tools and expertise needed to accelerate innovation and strengthen the domestic semiconductor supply chain,” said Synopsys&#8217; Salomone.</p>
<p>A major part of the MMEC’s work is helping regional entrepreneurs survive the so-called “Valley of Death” by giving members access to infrastructure capabilities, such as compute environments and design tools, at lower costs or through different cost models than has been available before. “Streamlining access to prototyping capabilities, whether that be tools to do epitaxial development, or the ability to do advanced packaging and module development and characterization and tests,” Casto said. “Even the access models that allow the demonstration of those in, say, relevant operational environments. We work closely with both the commercial and government sector, and even special labs and test ranges that will qualify and test those capabilities.”</p>
<p>This helps address one of the biggest needs for many startups in the Midwest — access to the tools that already exist in the region. “We are working with those companies in terms of developing intellectual property, which will make it easier for other companies to use the foundry ecosystems,” Casto said. “We&#8217;ve received a lot of feedback from those organizations and how they do their designs, and we&#8217;ve built those capabilities into our digital infrastructure at MMEC, so they can leverage those to be more competitive in the market. We can aggregate requirements and lower costs through economies of scale for other businesses to use. It really is a win-win environment as MMEC has scaled.”</p>

		<title>Beyond Scaling: The Growing Role Of Materials Innovation In Semiconductor Manufacturing</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/beyond-scaling-the-growing-role-of-materials-innovation-in-semiconductor-manufacturing/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/beyond-scaling-the-growing-role-of-materials-innovation-in-semiconductor-manufacturing/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Hideaki Okamoto]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:06:17 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Expanding computational capabilities and deeper co-development are changing how materials move from lab to fab.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/beyond-scaling-the-growing-role-of-materials-innovation-in-semiconductor-manufacturing/">Beyond Scaling: The Growing Role Of Materials Innovation In Semiconductor Manufacturing</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>For decades, semiconductor progress has been defined primarily by our ability to make devices smaller, faster and more powerful. But as the industry moves deeper into the AI era, scaling is becoming increasingly dependent on something less visible: the materials that make each new generation of devices possible.</p>
<p>This shift is already apparent across many semiconductor manufacturing trends. Advanced-node scaling is creating requirements that existing materials cannot always satisfy. AI is driving extraordinary demand for compute performance while simultaneously increasing data movement and power consumption. Electrical interconnects are approaching practical limitations, while power delivery and thermal challenges are becoming system-level constraints. As a result, the future of semiconductor manufacturing will depend not simply on optimizing existing materials, but increasingly on developing and commercializing fundamentally different ones.</p>
<p>This is not unique to semiconductors. Across industries, materials transitions have historically enabled major technological advances—from new battery chemistries to successive generations of displays. What is changing is the speed at which those transitions are occurring. Two forces in particular are accelerating materials innovation: rapidly expanding computational capabilities and a shift from conventional supplier relationships toward deeper co-development across the technology ecosystem. For semiconductor makers, the combination could fundamentally change how advanced materials move from the laboratory into high-volume manufacturing.</p>
<h2>Computational materials development</h2>
<p>Materials development has traditionally been an experimental discipline. Researchers synthesized a candidate material, characterized it, learned from the results and repeated the process. For complex materials, synthesizing a single candidate can take weeks, making extensive physical experimentation inherently slow.</p>
<p>Increasing computational power has changed that equation. Simulation can now take place before synthesis, allowing researchers to determine which candidates warrant physical experimentation. As models, proprietary data sets and computational resources improve, researchers can screen increasingly large numbers of candidates and identify regions of material performance that existing approaches simply cannot reach.</p>
<p>This distinction is important. The value of computational materials development is not limited to finding a better version of an existing material. It can reveal when incremental improvement is unlikely to meet the target at all.</p>
<p>That knowledge can shorten development cycles by enabling researchers to abandon an unproductive material path earlier and redirect resources toward a fundamentally new solution. The progression from supplementary calculation to pre-experiment screening, hyper-screening and ultimately materials AI illustrates how computing is becoming embedded throughout the discovery process.</p>
<p>For advanced semiconductor manufacturing, this capability will become increasingly valuable. Advanced node scaling materials must satisfy multiple—and sometimes conflicting—requirements involving electrical performance, thermal behavior, mechanical properties, purity, process compatibility and manufacturability. The search space is simply becoming too large for traditional trial-and-error development alone.</p>
<p>The next step will be combining accumulated experimental knowledge with high-performance computing, materials AI and, eventually, quantum computing. The organizations best positioned to capitalize on these tools may be those with something AI itself cannot manufacture overnight: large quantities of high-quality, proprietary materials data accumulated through decades of real-world development.</p>
<h2>Collaboration is critical</h2>
<p>Computational power alone, however, cannot solve the semiconductor industry’s materials challenges. The second major change is organizational. Semiconductor development has evolved from relatively linear customer-supplier relationships toward much more integrated collaboration among device makers, equipment companies and materials suppliers. That trend reflects the growing interdependence of process, equipment and materials performance.</p>
<p>When a new material must work within a deposition process, interact correctly with adjacent films and ultimately deliver a specific device characteristic, optimizing it independently makes less and less sense.</p>
<p>This argues for earlier supplier engagement and more extensive semiconductor roadmap collaboration. Instead of developing a material internally and presenting it to customers late in the process, materials suppliers can work with ecosystem partners while requirements and process architectures are still evolving.</p>
<p>Such partnerships offer another benefit that is difficult to replicate digitally: access to tacit knowledge. Formal specifications describe what a material needs to accomplish, but engineers working together often uncover process interactions, tradeoffs and practical constraints that never appear in a data sheet. Sharing that knowledge can substantially accelerate development.</p>
<p>It may also require changing how development resources are allocated. Traditional risk-reduction models increase investment gradually as technical uncertainty declines. A partnership-driven approach does nearly the opposite: it commits greater resources earlier, creating enough differentiated material candidates to engage partners sooner and accelerate the path toward a manufacturable solution. In that sense, materials co-innovation in semiconductors is becoming as much a strategic capability as a technical one.</p>
<h2>Where the next materials transitions may occur</h2>
<p>The emerging challenges around AI illustrate why this model matters. One example is the transition from wet to dry processes for increasingly fine-pitch semiconductor structures. Continued device miniaturization can require new precursors for thin-film deposition, creating a materials challenge that combines molecular design, computational screening and process expertise. Fine-pitch precursor development is an example of this intersection between performance requirements, simulation and collaborative process development.</p>
<p>But AI semiconductor materials requirements extend well beyond transistor fabrication.</p>
<p>Data movement is becoming a major constraint on computing performance and energy consumption. As electrical signaling speeds increase, power requirements rise sharply, strengthening the case for optical circuits and photonic interconnects. Optical circuits are a route to significantly reducing data-center power consumption, while high-speed optical modulation is becoming critical to scaling interconnect bandwidth.</p>
<p>These architectures create new materials opportunities—from transparent optical waveguide materials to organic electro-optic materials capable of extremely high-speed signal conversion. Here again, molecular design and proprietary materials databases can help explore combinations of optical performance, processability and reliability that would be difficult to optimize experimentally alone.</p>
<p>Power electronics represent another frontier. Rising data-center power demand is increasing the importance of more efficient power conversion. Gallium nitride (GaN) offers the potential for lower on-resistance, high-voltage operation and reduced power loss compared with conventional silicon approaches, but realizing those advantages at scale requires high-quality, cost-effective GaN substrate materials. Simulation-driven GaN process innovation is aimed at combining high-voltage performance, high-speed switching, low power loss and scalable substrate production.</p>
<p>These examples point toward a broader change in advanced materials trends for semiconductors. Materials can no longer be viewed simply as inputs selected after a device or process architecture has been established. Increasingly, the capabilities of available materials will help determine which architectures are feasible in the first place.</p>
<p>That changes the role of the materials supplier. The strategic materials partner of the future will need to understand market requirements early, maintain deep technology platforms, use advanced computational tools to explore enormous design spaces, and engage across the semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem before solutions are fully defined.</p>
<p>Semiconductor progress has always depended on materials innovation. What is different now is the pace, complexity and degree of collaboration required. As computing itself becomes a tool for discovering the materials that will enable the next generation of computing, a reinforcing cycle is emerging: better semiconductors increase computational power; greater computational power accelerates materials discovery; and new materials enable better semiconductors.</p>
<p>That cycle may prove to be one of the most important engines of semiconductor innovation in the decade ahead.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/beyond-scaling-the-growing-role-of-materials-innovation-in-semiconductor-manufacturing/">Beyond Scaling: The Growing Role Of Materials Innovation In Semiconductor Manufacturing</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>AI&#8217;s Storage Problem Is a Packaging Problem</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/ais-storage-problem-is-a-packaging-problem/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/ais-storage-problem-is-a-packaging-problem/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Chiung Lee]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:05:40 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Chip, Package, System]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[3D NAND]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[advanced packaging]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Amkor]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[hybrid bonding]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[NAND]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[storage]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281558</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>How thinner dies, taller stacks, and hybrid bonding are carrying NAND into the AI era.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ais-storage-problem-is-a-packaging-problem/">AI&#8217;s Storage Problem Is a Packaging Problem</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Most conversations about AI start and end with compute. But every training run and every inference query is ultimately a data problem, and data must live somewhere. Memory, and increasingly, the packaging that makes dense memory manufacturable, is doing as much to define AI system performance as the accelerators getting all the attention.</p>
<p>AI models, cloud services, smart devices and connected systems create, process and store information at rates that would have seemed implausible a decade ago. Storage has quietly become foundational infrastructure. Consumer devices generate data continuously, from sensors to entertainment platforms. Automotive systems, particularly autonomous and connected vehicles, depend on massive volumes of stored information simply to operate safely. The result is structural, long-term demand for NAND flash rather than another consumer-driven cycle.</p>
<h2>The everyday math of a data-hungry world</h2>
<p>The growth is easy to see in ordinary digital experiences. Moving a two-hour movie from HD (1080p) to 4K increases the data required by roughly 4.7X, driven by pixel density, the added bit depth needed for HDR, and higher frame-rate targets. Photography tells a similar story: image file sizes have grown about 3X as smartphone cameras went from 12MP to 48MP, with enhanced color processing and expanded dynamic range compounding the effect. Audio has followed, a three-minute track that can grow up to 6X moving from compressed MP3 to immersive formats such as Dolby Atmos.</p>
<p>Codec advances help. They don&#8217;t keep pace. Memory scaling must carry the rest.</p>
<h2>AI is redrawing the memory map</h2>
<p>Yole Group&#8217;s 2024 data put the stand-alone memory market at $170 billion, a 78% year-over-year rebound after two years of decline. DRAM, including HBM, accounted for roughly 57% of revenue; NAND took 40%.</p>
<p>Heading into 2026, AI workloads are reshaping how suppliers allocate capacity. Manufacturers are expanding production of HBM and advanced DRAM nodes, prioritizing products aligned to AI performance requirements, and accelerating HBM ramps that now represent more than 10% of the total memory market. That strengthens the HBM ecosystem, but it also constrains investment in traditional DRAM and NAND capacity.</p>
<p>NAND demand, meanwhile, keeps broadening: data center SSDs as critical storage infrastructure for AI servers; rising SSD attach rates across PCs and laptops; higher storage tiers in premium smartphones; and automotive systems where electrification and intelligent vehicle architectures require robust solid-state storage. Diversified demand supports a stable NAND outlook through 2026, even against tighter supply.</p>
<h2>From 50 packages to one</h2>
<p>The scaling story is best told in footprint. Storing 2TB in 2010, when only planar 2D NAND existed, would have taken more than 50 eMMC chips, each in a package roughly 17 x 22 mm. 3D NAND arrived in 2013 and changed the trajectory by stacking cells vertically; by 2020, 100+ layer architectures had sharply reduced the package count needed for the same capacity.</p>
<p>Next comes wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, which raises interconnect density while improving electrical performance at the wafer level. It is expected to push vertical scaling well past today&#8217;s devices, toward architectures that may eventually reach 800 to 1,000 layers through multi-wafer stacking. Combined with growing QLC adoption, higher-layer 3D NAND is enabling a single eMMC device to hit 2TB.</p>
<h2>Thin, tall and reliable: the packaging problem</h2>
<p>At the package level, mobile and enterprise SSD growth is driving denser BGA packages and faster interfaces, which in turn demand tightly integrated die stacks and controller integration. Getting dies thin enough to stack higher, without giving up yield or reliability, requires coordination across the entire flow, from wafer prep through final assembly.</p>
<p><strong>Wafer preparation. </strong>Modern flows are engineered for 300+ layer NAND, managing die stress and warpage to prevent cracking and chipping. Key capabilities include laser grooving, ultra-fine wafer grinding, blade or stealth dicing, and automated optical inspection for crack detection. Wafers thin from roughly 700–800 µm down to as little as 25–50 µm, at which point fine grinding, polishing and backside treatments become essential to remove subsurface micro-cracks and reduce stress concentrations. Saw streets are conditioned via laser grooving or plasma pre-cut, and techniques such as dice-before-grind (DBG) and stealth dice-before-grind (SDBG) minimize edge damage. AOI runs throughout, catching cracks before compromised dies reach assembly.</p>
<p><strong>Die handling. </strong>As dies gets thinner, conventional handling breaks down, literally. Specialized thin-die tooling, including needle-less pickup with precisely controlled vacuum force, is required to minimize bending and prevent fracture.</p>
<p><strong>Wire bond architecture. </strong>At 32+ die stacks, the challenge shifts from optimizing individual steps to managing the stack as a system. Ultra-low and ultra-long loop profiles maintain clearance in tall stacks, while extended die overhang supports stair-step and zig-zag configurations. Stair-step layouts protect wire clearance; zigzag distributes stress. Customized die attach, film-on-die (FOD), film-on-wire (FOW) or spacers, prevents die sag and preserves bond integrity in controller-under-NAND configurations without adding Z-height. All of this happens inside a shrinking Z budget dictated by end applications like smartphones.</p>
<p><strong>Molding and warpage control. </strong>Advanced compression molding minimizes flow-induced wire sweep and distributes pressure uniformly across tall stacks. Mold cap thickness and overall material balance must be optimized against profile targets while controlling CTE mismatch. Low-stress die-attach films, carefully selected substrates and optional EMI shielding round out the materials strategy.</p>
<p><strong>Inspection and data analytics. </strong>Inline inspection at key stages plus unit-level traceability create the feedback loop that sustains yield — enabling early anomaly detection, rapid correlation to materials, tools or process conditions, and faster excursion containment in high-volume production.</p>
<h2>Why the OSAT role is growing</h2>
<p>Not every NAND maker is an IDM able to own the full value chain from IP and wafer fab through final assembly and test. That gap is where OSATs matter, and in today&#8217;s geopolitical environment, globally distributed manufacturing has become a strategic asset rather than a logistics footnote.</p>
<p>Leading OSATs support consumer, industrial and automotive customers with high-stack memory packaging, unit-level traceability, wafer-level fan-out and turnkey test. Only a limited number operate true multi-region networks. As semiconductor companies prioritize diversified, geopolitically balanced supply chains, facilities spanning Asia, Europe and the United States are becoming a differentiator.</p>
<h2>The takeaway</h2>
<p>Data growth across consumer electronics, automotive, enterprise and cloud keeps raising the stakes for NAND. Meeting that demand takes progress on two fronts at once — device density and packaging technology. Hybrid bonding, taller die stacks and tighter reliability controls are what turn capacity roadmaps into shippable products.</p>
<p>Learn more about Amkor’s <a href="https://amkor.com/packaging/memory/">memory and storage solutions</a>.</p>

		<title>Driving Power Delivery Innovations For The AI Data Center</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/driving-power-delivery-innovations-for-the-ai-data-center/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/driving-power-delivery-innovations-for-the-ai-data-center/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Intel Foundry]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:04:55 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Whitepapers]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI data centers]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[backside power delivery]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[BPD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[integrated voltage regulator]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Intel Foundry]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[power delivery]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281377</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>As AI systems scale, advanced power delivery innovations are becoming critical to performance, efficiency and reliability.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/driving-power-delivery-innovations-for-the-ai-data-center/">Driving Power Delivery Innovations For The AI Data Center</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p style="font-weight: 400;">As AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads continue to scale, rising current demands are pushing traditional power delivery networks to their limits. Power delivery has become a critical challenge for modern computing systems, with current-density limitations, routing congestion and the growing complexity of multi-chip architectures creating new performance and reliability concerns.</p>
<p style="font-weight: 400;">This paper explores how power delivery requirements are evolving across the accelerator, rack and data center hierarchy. It examines Intel Foundry&#8217;s power delivery innovations, including Intel 18A backside power delivery and advanced silicon capacitor technologies that improve power integrity at the die and package levels. It also highlights Intel&#8217;s advancements in integrated voltage regulator (IVR) technology, which moves power conversion closer to the point of load within the package to help address current-density scaling challenges.</p>
<p style="font-weight: 400;">Rather than prescribing a single solution, the paper presents a range of approaches that architects and technologists can apply based on system requirements, performance objectives and architectural tradeoffs.</p>
<p style="font-weight: 400;"><strong>What You&#8217;ll Learn</strong></p>
<ul style="font-weight: 400;">
<li>Understand the key power delivery challenges shaping AI accelerators, racks and data center architectures.</li>
<li>Explore advanced power delivery innovations, including backside power delivery, silicon capacitors and integrated voltage regulators designed to improve efficiency and reliability.</li>
<li>Learn how to evaluate power delivery strategies and architectural tradeoffs for next-generation AI systems.</li>
</ul>
<p style="font-weight: 400;">Read <a href="https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/central-libraries/us/en/documents/2026-08/foundry-power-delivery-white-paper.pdf">more here</a>.</p>

		<title>Virtual Fabrication Meets Stress Physics: Solving GAA Channel Non-Uniformity</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/virtual-fabrication-meets-stress-physics-solving-gaa-channel-non-uniformity/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/virtual-fabrication-meets-stress-physics-solving-gaa-channel-non-uniformity/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Swapnil Kailash More]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:04:20 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[etch]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[GAA FETs]]></category>
