		<category><![CDATA[virtual fabrication]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281545</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Even small imbalances between stacked nanosheets can distort device behavior in ways that are difficult to predict from geometry alone.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/virtual-fabrication-meets-stress-physics-solving-gaa-channel-non-uniformity/">Virtual Fabrication Meets Stress Physics: Solving GAA Channel Non-Uniformity</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><a href="https://newsroom.lamresearch.com/everything-about-akara?blog=true">Gate-all-around (GAA)</a> nanosheet transistors are revolutionizing sub-5-nm CMOS chips, but a subtle design challenge has come into focus: the mechanical stress created in the nanosheet channels does not distribute uniformly across stacked GAA transistors.</p>
<p>Because stress reshapes the silicon band structure and directly changes carrier mobility,<sup>1</sup> even small imbalances between the stacked nanosheets can distort device behavior in ways that are difficult to predict from geometry alone.</p>
<h2>What causes stress non-uniformity in GAA transistors?</h2>
<p>Stress non-uniformity occurs when stacked nanosheet channels experience different strain levels during fabrication. These differences affect carrier mobility, current flow, threshold voltage, and leakage. Using SEMulator3D stress modeling, engineers can identify these variations early and optimize channel thickness, fin width, and lateral etch to improve performance.</p>
<p>To illustrate, imagine that a GAA transistor’s stacked channels are three parallel highway lanes meant to carry traffic evenly. If one lane is smoother or wider than the others, more cars naturally shift into it. Similarly, if one nanosheet has higher stress and better carrier mobility, it could carry a disproportionate share of current, throwing off the device’s expected behavior.</p>
<p>Fixing this stress problem requires a tool that can emulate a sequence of semiconductor fabrication steps and proactively identify stress problems in the resulting three-dimensional structure.</p>
<p>Lam <a href="https://www.lamresearch.com/semiverse-solutions/?highlight=semiverse">Semiverse Solutions</a> engineers used <a href="https://www.lamresearch.com/product/semulator3d/">SEMulator3D</a> with integrated stress modeling to predict stress variations across GAA stacked nanosheets and learn how to improve stress uniformity. They identified how channel thickness, fin width, and lateral etch interact to drive non-uniform stress, revealing that a slightly thicker top channel dramatically improves uniformity.</p>
<h2>Why stress uniformity is critical for GAA nanosheet transistor performance</h2>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281546" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig1.webp?resize=785%2C664&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="785" height="664" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig1.webp?w=785&amp;ssl=1 785w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C254&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C650&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C508&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 785px) 100vw, 785px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Gate-all-around field-effect transistor architecture.</strong></p>
<p>A GAA architecture consists of isolated silicon channels stacked vertically between the source and drain. The channels are wrapped by the gate, which controls electron transport and the on/off state of the transistor. Stress or strain in the channels reshapes the silicon band structure and the carrier mobility, saturation current, off-state current, and threshold voltage.</p>
<p>Ideally, all GAA channels see identical stress and behave identically. In practice, process-induced variations cause them to see different stress or strain levels. The highest-stressed channel exhibits enhanced mobility and carries a disproportionate share of the current. A high-strain, low-Vt (threshold voltage) nanosheet channel can dominate off-state leakage, even if the other channels remain well controlled. This leakage current can create a spread in Vt and modify the effective turn-on characteristic of the transistor in unexpected ways. Uniform stress across the stack is therefore a critical design target, and simulation is essential because it is not obvious at the outset how to achieve it.</p>
<h2>Simulate stress in GAA nanosheet devices</h2>
<p>We created a 3D process model of the GAA device by inputting layout, process step,<sup>2,3</sup> and material information into SEMulator3D. We then explored predicted stress levels in the GAA channels using the generated 3D model with integrated stress analysis.</p>
<p>Stress is generated in the channels because of lattice mismatch between silicon and the epitaxially grown source and drain regions. For the pFET, the epitaxially grown source/drain material has a slightly greater lattice constant than silicon. The nFET source/drain material has a slightly smaller lattice constant than silicon.</p>
<p>During the replacement-metal-gate (RMG) process steps, the channels become freestanding, which allows these stressors to relax. The compressively stressed source/drain regions expand and push the pFET channels into compression, while the tensile stressed source/drain regions contract and pull the nFET channels into tension (see Figure 2).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281547" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig2.webp?resize=556%2C719&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="556" height="719" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig2.webp?w=556&amp;ssl=1 556w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig2.webp?resize=232%2C300&amp;ssl=1 232w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 556px) 100vw, 556px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Stress transfer to the silicon channel during the fabrication process.</strong></p>
<p>In the model, stress is solved during every major process step change: the epitaxial Si/SiGe stack, fin patterning, the gate module, source/drain growth, and the RMG module.</p>
<h2>How channel thickness influences stress uniformity in GAA nanosheets</h2>
<p>We executed a Design of Experiments (DOE) to test the impact of design changes on stress uniformity. The DOE varied the individual silicon layer thicknesses (Channel 1 to 3 thickness) and the fin width. Together, these parameters control the channel cross-section area, the primary driver of stress.</p>
<p>We extracted the average longitudinal stress (Sigma_yy) along a vertical cut of the channels (Figure 3). Three clear peaks of stress magnitude are shown, which correspond to the three nanosheets used in our model. These stress peaks are compressive for the pFET and tensile for the nFET. The three values are visibly different, with the nFET demonstrating larger stress non-uniformity or variability.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281548" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig3.webp?resize=1386%2C499&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1386" height="499" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig3.webp?w=1386&amp;ssl=1 1386w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig3.webp?resize=300%2C108&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig3.webp?resize=1024%2C369&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig3.webp?resize=768%2C277&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig3.webp?resize=600%2C216&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Control parameters for the DoE and the Sigma_yy along the z-cut of the channels for both pFET and nFET.</strong></p>
<p>Figure 4 represents stress non-uniformity (referred to as “stress difference”) using a contour plot as a function of the DOE variables. The stress difference for the pFET stays under 200 MPa, while the nFET stress difference reaches 400 to 800 MPa. The stress difference is most sensitive to the topmost channel’s (Channel 3) thickness. As Channel 3’s thickness increases, the stress difference decreases.</p>
<p>This is seen in Figure 4, as Channel 3’s thickness increases from 4 nm to 7 nm, and the red (highest stress difference) contours change to blue (lowest stress difference). This result indicates that the topmost channel (Channel 3) needs to be slightly thicker than the channels below to minimize the stress difference among channels.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281549" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig4.webp?resize=974%2C458&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="974" height="458" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig4.webp?w=974&amp;ssl=1 974w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig4.webp?resize=300%2C141&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig4.webp?resize=768%2C361&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig4.webp?resize=600%2C282&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 974px) 100vw, 974px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 4: Top channel thickness contributes most to stress non-uniformity.</strong></p>
<h2>How fin width and lateral etch affect GAA stress uniformity</h2>
<p>The impact of fin width becomes pronounced when the fin lateral-etch ratio is high (Figure 5). The fin width is measured at the shallow trench isolation (STI) elevation for reference. The fin lateral etch ratio controls the fin taper and determines the channel width loss above the STI elevation.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281550" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig5.webp?resize=849%2C752&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="849" height="752" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig5.webp?w=849&amp;ssl=1 849w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig5.webp?resize=300%2C266&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig5.webp?resize=768%2C680&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig5.webp?resize=600%2C531&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 849px) 100vw, 849px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 5: The impact of fin lateral etch on the channel width.</strong></p>
<p>At a low lateral etch ratio, the fin taper is low, and channel width variation is not significant. At high lateral etch, the top channel becomes significantly narrower than the bottom. The interaction of fin width and fin lateral etch, for stress non-uniformity, is seen in Figure 6.</p>
<p>At a lower lateral etch ratio of 0.05 and 0.075, the stress difference contours do not change much as the fin width is reduced. At a higher lateral etch ratio of 0.1 (larger fin taper), the stress difference contours change as fin width changes. Specifically, for a narrow fin (25 to 26 nm) and thin channel 3 (4 to 5 nm), the stress difference in the nFET case is 900 MPa. If the fin width is fixed at 25 nm and Channel 3’s thickness is increased from 4 nm to 7 nm, the stress difference falls close to 500 MPa. The effect is weaker for the pFET but still present under an excessive lateral etch ratio.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281553" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig6.webp?resize=974%2C779&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="974" height="779" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig6.webp?w=974&amp;ssl=1 974w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig6.webp?resize=300%2C240&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig6.webp?resize=768%2C614&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Lam_Virtual-Fab-Meets-Stress-Physics-GAA-fig6.webp?resize=600%2C480&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 974px) 100vw, 974px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 6: Evolution of stress difference contours as a function of fin width and channel 3 thickness for different fin lateral etch ratios.</strong></p>
<h2>Key takeaways for GAA nanosheet stress optimization</h2>
<p>This study underscores the value of SEMulator3D beyond its use as a 3D process model builder or discrete process modeling tool. By emulating the full sequence of <a href="https://www.lamresearch.com/products/our-processes/deposition/">deposition</a>, <a href="https://www.lamresearch.com/products/our-solutions/patterning-solutions/?highlight=patterning">patterning</a>, and gate-module steps and then solving for stress on the resulting 3D structure, it captures how subtle process choices impact device performance.</p>
<p>Spacer thickness, lateral etch, and individual channel thicknesses translate into mechanical variability across stacked nano-sheets. Coupling of complex semiconductor processing with high-fidelity stress simulation turns raw geometry into actionable design insight, allowing engineers to co-optimize channel thickness and fin width for uniform stress and predictable GAA device performance.</p>

		<title>From Silicon To Systems: Heterogeneous Integration As The Engine Of AI Performance</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/from-silicon-to-systems-heterogeneous-integration-as-the-engine-of-ai-performance/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/from-silicon-to-systems-heterogeneous-integration-as-the-engine-of-ai-performance/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Lalitha Immaneni]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:02:44 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Foundry Focus]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[advanced packaging]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[chiplets]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[design space exploration]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[heterogeneous integration]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Intel Foundry]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281539</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Design space exploration must become a core capability for advanced packaging and chiplet-based systems. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/from-silicon-to-systems-heterogeneous-integration-as-the-engine-of-ai-performance/">From Silicon To Systems: Heterogeneous Integration As The Engine Of AI Performance</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>We are in the middle of one of the most important shifts our industry has seen in decades. The internet economy transformed how people connect, communicate, and consume information. The AI economy is redefining a more fundamental layer: how compute is architected, delivered, scaled, and optimized. AI workloads are creating demands for power, memory bandwidth, I/O, thermal performance, and system-level efficiency that traditional silicon scaling alone cannot satisfy.</p>
<p>In my SKYTalk at the Design Automation Conference (DAC) 2026, I shared that meeting this moment requires expanding our frame of innovation beyond silicon alone to the full system: silicon, package, board, platform, software, and the ecosystem that brings them together. Through 18 papers and posters at the conference, our Intel engineers showcased research spanning advanced packaging, AI-enabled design, verification, and system technology co-optimization (STCO), highlighting innovations that help optimize and scale increasingly complex 3DIC, chiplet-based, and heterogeneous systems.</p>
<h2>Advanced packaging becomes an architectural foundation</h2>
<p>This shift is putting advanced packaging at the center of the next era of performance. For many years, packaging was viewed primarily as the final step in semiconductor manufacturing to protect the die, connect it to the board, and help remove heat. That role has changed dramatically. Today, advanced packaging is no longer just an integration step. It is becoming an architectural foundation. It enables us to connect chiplets, integrate memory and high-speed I/O, manage power and thermals, and build systems that would not be practical or possible as monolithic silicon.</p>
<p>The industry has already embraced chiplets and heterogeneous integration as powerful tools. By disaggregating a monolithic design into functional chiplets, we can mix and match design blocks, process nodes, foundries, and technologies to optimize performance, cost, yield, and time to market. This approach enables products that can exceed reticle limits, reuse IP more efficiently, and align each function with the process technology best suited to its requirements. But chiplets alone are not the end goal. The real opportunity comes when we move beyond a chiplet mindset to a systems mindset.</p>
<p>For AI, this systems mindset is essential. AI architectures do not allow us to optimize the die, package, and board in isolation. The performance vectors are too interdependent. Thermal behavior influences architecture choices. Power delivery affects performance headroom. Mechanical constraints affect yield and reliability. Memory integration and high-speed I/O affect the entire product landing zone. If we cannot model, explore, verify, and close these interactions across silicon, package, and system, we do not fully unlock the value of the technologies we are developing. Technology opens possibilities. Design enablement creates reality.</p>
<h2>Design space exploration in the AI era</h2>
<p>This is why design space exploration must become a core capability for advanced packaging and chiplet-based systems. It provides a structured way to evaluate architectural trade-offs and identify the optimal product landing zone using validated models, tools, and methodologies. It spans decisions across architecture, connectivity, packaging, and manufacturing. Teams must determine how functionality should be partitioned, which process technologies to use, and how dies will communicate within the package. At the same time, they need to balance system-level considerations such as power delivery, thermal performance, memory integration, and high-speed I/O while ensuring the design can be manufactured and scaled with strong yield. None of these choices can be made independently. The value comes from understanding the trade-offs early, before the cost of change becomes too high.</p>
<p>A key example is die-to-die IP. Chiplet architectures depend on physical and functional connectivity between dies, and that connectivity must be co-designed with the package. Success depends on getting details right, from bump pitch and bump maps to package compatibility, electrical performance, and validation using real test silicon. Looking beyond a single product, widespread chiplet adoption will require a much broader ecosystem. Interoperable die-to-die IP, package technologies, process nodes, foundries, design kits, standards, and IP providers must work together seamlessly. Interoperability is not a nice-to-have. It is a requirement if we want heterogeneous integration to scale.</p>
<p>Thermals and mechanics are another example of why system-level optimization is now mandatory. AI workloads can sustain near-peak activity, creating new thermal challenges and localized hot spots. On-package integration increases power density, and the package must increasingly support thermal strategies that reach into the system level. That means thermal analysis must happen early, beginning at architecture definition, and continue through IP planning, silicon floorplanning, package layout, and system design. Experimentally calibrated models, material characterization, and continuous feedback are essential to making those analyses accurate and actionable.</p>
<p>Power delivery must be treated with the same level of system thinking. Performance headroom starts in the package. The placement of decoupling capacitance and other power delivery ingredients across die, package, and system have a direct impact on product capability. As these systems grow more complex, connecting physical understanding with design enablement becomes increasingly critical.</p>
<h2>From sequential design to concurrent system co-optimization</h2>
<p>These challenges also expose the limitations of the traditional sequential design model. Historically, chip, package, and board teams could work in a largely serial flow, synchronizing at key boundaries such as bump maps and package footprints. That model breaks down for AI systems. Today, we need concurrent design across chiplets, package, board, and system. We must optimize together for performance, cost, yield, time to market, form factor, reliability, and manufacturability. The package cannot be treated as a downstream constraint. It must be part of the architecture from the start. Enabling that level of concurrent optimization requires more sophisticated modeling and simulation capabilities than traditional design flows can provide.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281541" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Hetero-Integration-Engine-AI-Performance-fig1.webp?resize=1174%2C486&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1174" height="486" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Hetero-Integration-Engine-AI-Performance-fig1.webp?w=1174&amp;ssl=1 1174w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Hetero-Integration-Engine-AI-Performance-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C124&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Hetero-Integration-Engine-AI-Performance-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C424&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Hetero-Integration-Engine-AI-Performance-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C318&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Hetero-Integration-Engine-AI-Performance-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C248&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Advanced packaging increasingly relies on concurrent co-design and verification across silicon, package, and board domains.</strong></p>
<p>Digital twins and multiphysics modeling will be increasingly important in this transformation. As systems become larger and more complex, we need better ways to predict outcomes, compare configurations, and reduce risk before committing to expensive prototypes. A digital twin can create a virtual representation of a physical system, connect design and process data, and support simulation and predictive analytics. Used well, these capabilities create a continuous learning loop that improves each generation of products and helps teams make better architecture-wide decisions earlier.</p>
<h2>Building the ecosystem for heterogeneous integration</h2>
<p>At Intel, our role is not only to develop advanced packaging technologies. It is to help enable the ecosystem required to use those technologies successfully. That includes a broad set of technology building blocks, from Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB), Foveros, redistribution layer (RDL)-based interposers, and 2.5D and 3D integration technologies. Equally important are the supporting capabilities, including package assembly design kits, electronic design automation (EDA) tools and flows, standards for modularity and integration, certified IP for advanced packaging, and design service partners who can help customers move from early architecture to tapeout. Design enablement from early concept through product execution is what turns technology options into customer solutions.</p>
<p>Success in heterogeneous integration ultimately depends on the strength of the broader industry ecosystem. Foundries, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) companies, EDA vendors, IP providers, memory suppliers, technology providers, and customers all have to work together. STCO needs to become part of our DNA. It requires architectural, physical, manufacturing, verification, power, thermal, and performance considerations to be connected from the beginning. No single company or discipline can solve this alone. This is a team sport, and every part of the ecosystem has a role to play.</p>
<p>The call to action is simple: adopt a system-first design mindset. Design the system. Optimize together. Scale through collaboration. As AI products continue to grow in complexity, we will need fast, real-time, seamless, integrated analysis and design flows that can keep pace with the scale of the challenge. Advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration give us the foundation. But design enablement, ecosystem collaboration, standards, validated IP, and concurrent system design will determine how fully we can realize their potential.</p>
<p>AI is changing the rules of compute. Our opportunity is to change how we architect, design, and enable the systems that power it. The next era of performance will not be defined by silicon alone. It will be defined by how well we integrate, optimize, and collaborate from silicon to systems.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/from-silicon-to-systems-heterogeneous-integration-as-the-engine-of-ai-performance/">From Silicon To Systems: Heterogeneous Integration As The Engine Of AI Performance</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Predicting Silicon Behavior Years Before Test Wafers</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/predicting-silicon-behavior-years-before-test-wafers/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/predicting-silicon-behavior-years-before-test-wafers/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Larry Melvin]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:01:51 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing Solutions]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[line-edge roughness]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[lithography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[lithography simulation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[simulation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Synopsys]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[test wafers]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281532</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Wafer-validated optical simulation for high-NA EUV applications.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/predicting-silicon-behavior-years-before-test-wafers/">Predicting Silicon Behavior Years Before Test Wafers</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Semiconductor engineers have known for decades that serial fabrication runs of test wafers is an inefficient way to bring up new processes and technologies. Modern deep submicron nodes have only reinforced this observation. It now costs several years and tens of billions of dollars just to build a fab. Every test wafer run takes months and costs millions. Finding problems after a run, figuring out the causes, devising fixes, and waiting for the next set of wafers to confirm the results is just not feasible anymore.</p>
<p>The only solution is an <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/glossary/what-is-electronic-design-automation.html">electronic design automation (EDA)</a> toolset that can accurately predict chip behavior before any wafers are run, and even before the fab is ready. This enables the very first test wafers to closely match the desired characteristics. It also minimizes the number of tweaks and fab runs needed to refine the process for production designs. <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/manufacturing/mask-solutions/s-litho.html">Synopsys S-Litho</a>, which provides early lithography pathfinding, process optimization, and analysis, is a prime example of such a solution. Recent results demonstrate dramatically the accuracy of its predictions years before test wafers are available.</p>
<h2>A prediction case study</h2>
<p>In 2021, Synopsys engineers used S-Litho to simulate high-NA (numerical aperture) EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography for a 22nm pitch. The analysis predicted about a 0.5 nm line width roughness (LWR) for horizontal (H) compared with vertical (V). Since line edge roughness (LER) is generally a bit more than half of LWR, the LER prediction was therefore around 0.3 nm for H compared to V. S-Litho also predicted a 50% failure rate reduction for H versus V lines. These predictions were published in May 2021 in the Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials, and Metrology<sup>1</sup>:</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281534" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig1.webp?resize=1200%2C675&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1200" height="675" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig1.webp?w=1200&amp;ssl=1 1200w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C576&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p>The prediction that vertical lines would have higher defectivity and LER than horizontal lines meant that lines would come out jagged instead of smooth, and even small deviations would impact performance greatly. Frankly, there was considerable industry skepticism at the time about these conclusions. Past experience had shown that in low-NA EUV lithography, horizontal lines exhibited higher defectivity and worse LER than vertical lines. At the time, not only were wafer results unavailable, but wafer fab equipment (WFE) was still in development. In fact, WFE manufacturers were among the skeptics.</p>
<h2>Silicon results</h2>
<p>It took several years for equipment to be developed, fabs to be built, and test wafers to be run. Actual 21 nm silicon results were presented by IBM at the International Conference on Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography<sup>2</sup> in 2025 and at Optical and EUV Nanolithography XXXIX<sup>3</sup> in 2026. These results showed that vertical lines had LER of 1.6 nm and horizontal lines LER of 1.3 nm, the 0.3 nm difference predicted four years earlier by S-Litho. The graphs below show the reported LER measurements for horizontal lines on the left and vertical lines on the right.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281535" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig2.webp?resize=1200%2C675&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1200" height="675" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig2.webp?w=1200&amp;ssl=1 1200w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C576&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Predict-Silicon-Behavior-Before-Test-Wafers-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p>In 21/22 nm high-NA EUV, the horizontal direction is illuminated at an angle, the Chief Ray Angle. This is necessary to use the Bragg reflector and keep the incoming and outgoing photons from interfering. Also, the illumination angle needs to be below roughly 12 degrees to keep the reflected intensity as high as possible. The horizontal direction has an 8X magnification, and the vertical direction has a 4X magnification.</p>
<p>Industry opinion in 2021 was that shadowing would degrade the horizontal direction performance, as observed in 0.33 NA EUV, where the vertical direction has better performance than the horizontal, but both have 4X magnification. The magnification impact on LER was thought to be less than the shadowing impact. Contrary to expectations, in high-NA EUV the magnification dominated, which S-Litho correctly predicted.</p>
<h2>Benefits of prediction</h2>
<p>S-Litho provides physics-based, end-to-end lithography simulation independent of WFE development and long before test wafer results. The IBM silicon measurements testify to the accuracy of S-Litho LER predictions. IBM could not (yet) report real-world failure rates since it takes millions of parts in production to establish a failure history. The ability of S-Litho to predict failure rates before test wafers, let alone full production, is highly valuable.</p>
<p>S-Litho&#8217;s power and accuracy have important benefits for the semiconductor industry. For advanced nodes with high-NA EUV lithography, early, trusted prediction reduces risk and guides process and design tradeoffs. It also informs the selection of hardware and software development tools. Accurate predictive simulation is a prerequisite for technology leadership.</p>
<p>These results also have positive implications for Synopsys Proteus full-chip mask synthesis smart manufacturing solutions. High-NA Proteus OPC (Optical Proximity Correction) was built and validated using S-Litho. Thus, chip developers can also count on Proteus results before silicon is available. The number of test wafer runs is dramatically reduced. If process tweaks are made, S-Litho can check to see if the desired effects will be achieved without waiting for a new fab run. As fab times continue to elongate, any reduction in test wafer runs saves enormous time and cost.</p>
<h2>Conclusion</h2>
<p>The ability to predict future lithography behavior has become a strategic enabler for semiconductor development. S-Litho is the first wafer-validated optical simulation solution for high-NA EUV applications. Process developers no longer have to wait for next-generation equipment or fabs. S-Litho is a key step toward the industry goal of having true digital twins for processes.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.synopsys.com/manufacturing/mask-solutions/s-litho.html">Learn more about S-Litho Predictive Lithography Simulation</a>.</p>
<h3>References</h3>

<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/predictive-tcad-modeling-of-normally-off-p-gan-hemts-for-dynamic-rdson-leakage-breakdown-and-ml-based-design-exploration/">Predictive TCAD Modeling of Normally-Off p-GaN HEMTs for Dynamic RDS(on), Leakage, Breakdown, and ML-Based Design Exploration</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<h3 class="p2"><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="wp-image-66494 alignright" src="https://i0.wp.com/silvaco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SS_Q3_SEP2026_image-web.jpg?resize=274%2C179&#038;ssl=1" sizes="auto, (max-width: 274px) 100vw, 274px" srcset="https://silvaco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SS_Q3_SEP2026_image-web.jpg 600w, https://silvaco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SS_Q3_SEP2026_image-web-300x196.jpg 300w, https://silvaco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SS_Q3_SEP2026_image-web-43x28.jpg 43w, https://silvaco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SS_Q3_SEP2026_image-web-63x41.jpg 63w, https://silvaco.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SS_Q3_SEP2026_image-web-48x31.jpg 48w" alt="" width="274" height="179" /><strong>Abstract</strong></h3>
<p class="p2">This article presents a practical simulation workflow for predictive simulation of normally-off p-GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs), with emphasis on device-physics calibration, leakage modeling, dynamic RDS(on), breakdown behavior, and machine-learning-assisted design exploration. The workflow is based on a 100 V p-GaN HEMT reference structure and combines process-informed device definition, careful meshing, calibrated Victory Device physics models, mixed-mode switching simulation, Design of Experiments (DOE), and Victory Analytics surrogate modeling. The goal is to establish a repeatable methodology that helps engineers understand how traps, polarization, Mg diffusion, electric-field distribution, and switching conditions influence GaN power-device performance and reliability.</p>
<p>Read <a href="https://silvaco.com/simulation-standard/predictive-tcad-modeling-of-normally-off-p-gan-hemts-for-dynamic-rdson-leakage-breakdown-and-ml-based-design-exploration/">more here</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/predictive-tcad-modeling-of-normally-off-p-gan-hemts-for-dynamic-rdson-leakage-breakdown-and-ml-based-design-exploration/">Predictive TCAD Modeling of Normally-Off p-GaN HEMTs for Dynamic RDS(on), Leakage, Breakdown, and ML-Based Design Exploration</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
